Let’s dive into Chapter 1: Rethinking the Way Problems Are Framed.
You know, most of us approach problems carrying a whole set of hidden assumptions—shaped by our experiences, our culture, even just our habits. Often, we don’t even realize they’re there. But these assumptions quietly guide our choices, and sometimes, they put blinders on us, making it tough to see all the possible solutions out there.
So, what’s the first step if you want to think differently? It’s simple, but not always easy: just pause for a second and take a closer look at how you’re defining the problem. Instead of jumping right into the obvious question, ask yourself—are we even asking the right question in the first place?
Picture this: a kid gets handed a puzzle for the very first time. No expectations, no idea what’s “supposed” to work. The child pokes, prods, maybe even turns the puzzle upside down. It’s pure curiosity—no limits, no fear of being wrong.
That’s the magic adults tend to lose. We show up with our mental toolkit, full of standard answers and a need to look smart. The problem is, that can mean we totally miss what’s really going on.
There’s a classic example: a city dealing with traffic congestion. The knee-jerk question is, “How can we build more roads to ease traffic?” But what if we dig deeper? What if we ask, “Why are so many people driving at the same time?” or “What incentives are making folks choose their cars over other options?”
Suddenly, different solutions pop up—maybe it’s about staggered work hours, or making public transit more appealing. By shifting the way we frame the problem, we unlock fresh ideas we’d have missed otherwise.
Now, this isn’t about being difficult just for the sake of it. It’s about understanding that the way you pose a question actually shapes the answers you end up with. If you start with the wrong question, even your best answer can lead you down the wrong path.
Here’s what reframing the problem looks like in practice:
First, step back and check the assumptions hiding behind the problem.
Second, think about whether the question you’re asking is really the most useful one.
And third, look for any hidden incentives or constraints that might be steering behavior in a certain direction.
So, what does this look like day-to-day? Well, let’s say your team keeps missing deadlines. The easy question is, “How can we get more done, faster?” But maybe the real questions are, “Are these deadlines even realistic?” or “What’s actually getting in our way?”
By challenging the original framing, you open up new ways to solve the problem—ways you might never have considered if you’d just stuck with the obvious question.
At the end of the day, making a habit of questioning the question is a key skill for anyone who wants to solve problems creatively. It takes humility, a bit of patience, and sometimes the courage to ask what everyone else assumes is settled.
But here’s the thing—those are often the questions that lead to breakthroughs others will miss.
